https://www.dw.com/en/thai-ex-lawmaker-s.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IXPx Authorities performed CPR on Thongchai Yenprasert, president of the Nonthaburi Provincial Administrative Organization, after he was shot Image: Talingchan520/Handout/REUTERS Advertisement Thai police arrested a suspected gunman — identified as former lawmaker Chalong Riewraeng — after he allegedly fired shots that killed a local politician on Monday at a government office on the outskirts of Bangkok. Authorities said the former MP confessed to the shooting. Surrounded by police, Chalong told reporters he attempted to speak with Thongchai Yenprasert about money. "I followed him to his car and hit his car's window, saying I want to talk," the suspect said. "He said he will not talk, so I pulled my gun. I did not aim to shoot, but his driver pulled a gun and pointed it at me so I fired." Thongchai, who was chairman of the Nonthaburi Provincial Administrative Organization, died of his wounds, according to Sakon Sukprom, director of Phra Nang Klao hospital. Thongchai's driver was also shot and successfully underwent surgery, Sakon added. Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul said no one in Thailand other than on-duty officials was allowed to carry a gun in public. He pointed out that the last gun-carry licences were issued three years ago and were only valid for one year. He said authorities will pursue "full legal action" against Chalong, a former member of the prime minister's party. "No matter who he is, he is now a murderer," Anutin said. Police: Shooting a 'personal issue' Nonthaburi Governor Chestha Mosikarat told reporters the suspect and victim were "friends for a long time" and the incident likely stemmed from a misunderstanding. Police said the motive for the shooting was a "personal issue." "According to his confession, it was about money that the ... chairman borrowed from him for several years, and he asked for the return of the money several times," regional Police Commander Wattana Yeechin told reporters, adding that the dispute was over several million baht (1 million baht is about €26,220 or $30,300). Second recent shooting This comes just days after a 14-year-old's shooting rampage, first at his home and then at the Debsirin Nonthaburi School, left nine people dead and over 20 injured. That incident was Thailand's deadliest mass shooting in nearly four years. Prime Minister Anutin had reiterated his intention to tighten gun control laws in the wake of the shooting. The Southeast Asian country's current gun laws do not include mental health screenings and allow people as young as 20 to have guns. Thailand had around 15 guns per 100 ⁠residents, the highest rate in Southeast Asia ​by a wide margin, according to a 2017 estimate by the Small Arms Survey. https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2.text: At least 47 people have been killed, according to the latest figures from officials, and dozens of buildings have collapsed in cities across western Colombia. The quake caused serious damage to buildings and prompted evacuations as far away as Bogota. People remain trapped in Cali, one of Colombia’s largest cities, after more than two dozen structures ‌collapsed, mayor Alejandro Eder said. ‌ He added that the city had asked authorities in Bogota and Medellin to send disaster teams ‌to support rescue efforts. Colombia’s Geological Service said that it had been “the highest magnitude earthquake registered in Colombia in the last decade” and that it had been followed by two 2.8 and 4.8 magnitude aftershocks. Authorities also reported that flights were suspended in the airports of Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago y Buenaventura and Pereira. Colombian president Abelardo de la Espriella said in a post on X that he will personally supervise recovery efforts and install an emergency centre

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c7v4.text: Image source, Reuters Image caption, Tristan and Andrew Tate pictured in April 2026 at Kaseya Center, Miami By Dan Sales Published 5 September 2026 Romanian prosecutors have officially indicted social media influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate with a range of trafficking and sex offences. They are accused of making more than $1.2m (Â£888,000) by coercing a girl to perform sex acts on video chats, according to the Romanian Directorate for Investigating Crime and Terrorism (DIICOT). Andrew, 39, is charged with trafficking minors, money laundering and having sex with a minor. Tristan, 38, is charged with complicity in trafficking in minors and money laundering. The Tates - currently in a Miami jail fighting extradition to the UK over separate charges - deny all the allegations. Will the Tate brothers be extradited from the US to the UK? Published 21 July The brothers - former kickboxers with dual US and British citizenship - have been under criminal investigation in Romania since December 2022. They have been mainly based there since 2017, drawing a large social media audience - many of them young men - through misogynistic messages and images of a luxury lifestyle. Romanian prosecutors described a case as centring on a vulnerable female who was 15 at the time of the alleged offence, in information released on Friday. She is alleged to have been recruited by Andrew and housed in a building in Luton, Bedfordshire, so he could sexually exploit her. Tristan is alleged to have been an accessory, prosecutors say, using physical aggression to coerce the victim. DIICOT investigators allege Andrew controlled her through surveillance and physical aggression, and coerced her to perform sex acts on video chats for his financial gain. Andrew is also accused of moving her to Romania to carry on exploiting her in two of his homes. He is separately charged with having sex with a minor, who was 15, in Romania. Prosecutors have also requested four of the brothers' luxury cars worth Â£710,000 be confiscated. They believe money was laundered through their purchase. The two brothers were previously indicted in Romania on trafficking charges, but in 2024 an appeals court in Bucharest sent the case back to prosecutors after deeming some evidence inadmissible. It is not yet clear if DIICOT will seek their extradition from the US and the indictment has to be examined by a judge before any trial can begin. The Tates have denied all the allegations and say their online personas are not their real personalities. Their lawyer in Romania, Eugen Constantin Vidineac, said: "Today's decision by DIICOT does not determine guilt and it should not be presented as though it does. It represents the prosecution's latest attempt to bring this case before a court following the failure of its previous indictment to proceed to trial. "The history of these proceedings matters. The previous indictment was subjected to judicial scrutiny and the court identified significant irregularities which prevented the case from moving forward to trial. "DIICOT has now chosen to file a new indictment. We will examine every aspect of it with the same level of scrutiny and we will challenge any evidential, procedural or legal deficiencies through the appropriate judicial process. "Our clients continue to reject the allegations against them. They have the right to the presumption of innocence, the right to properly examine the evidence relied upon against them and the right to mount an effective defence." Correction 5 September: A previous version of this article incorrectly stated that the Tate brothers were charged with further offences. The article has been updated to make clear they have been officially indicted with offences of which they had already been accused. It has also been updated to reflect that Andrew, not Tristan, was alleged to have recruited the 15-year-old. https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/14/russ.text: Russian state-owned companies spent more than three times as much on landline telephones in the first eight months this year as in the same period in 2025, as mobile internet shutdowns affecting nearly 80% of the country push ministries and businesses to seek alternatives to disrupted networks.Procurement data cited by the Russian business daily Vedomosti show spending at 118 million roubles (€1.26 million) from January through August, with the number of purchase tenders up 12.5%.Purchases are concentrated in the country’s largest business and infrastructure hubs.Market participants told Vedomosti that the surge was driven by the restrictions, a shift by Russian ministries and companies to domestically produced software-based PBX systems after Western vendors withdrew from the Russian market following the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, and demand for secure communications channels.Russia began systematically shutting down mobile internet access in May 2025, when services went offline in more than 40 regions ahead of Victory Day celebrations. What were initially episodic outages quickly became routine.An independent monitoring project recorded 655 mobile internet outages in June 2025, rising to 2,099 in July, a figure that exceeded the worldwide total for the entire previous year, according to analysts.The disruptions have hit banking, taxi services, food delivery and navigation, particularly in rural areas.The authorities have justified the shutdowns as a defence against Ukrainian drones, which they say are guided via mobile internet signals.Experts have disputed this, saying drones can fly preset routes without a network connection, and the shutdowns have reached regions far from the front line.In March, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the presidential administration “uses landline telephones” when asked how restrictions in central Moscow affect the work of the president’s office.Shortly after, head of state telecoms company Rostelecom Mikhail Oseyevsky urged Russians to return to fixed lines.“Like a fire extinguisher, there should be one in every home," Oseyevsky said.Russia has approximately 12.2 landline telephones per 100 residents. In Moscow, around 2 million households use fixed lines provided by MGTS, the city’s main telephone operator.Across the country, there are about 17.4 million urban household landline connections.The Ministry of Economic Development forecasts that the number of all landlines will fall to between 8.2 and 8.5 per 100 residents by 2029.
